_meta.author: Eduventure (original questions)
_meta.note: Pre-university batch 1: Mathematics 12, Physics 10, Chemistry 10, Biology 8, Economics 10. In review until approved in /admin. Contains answers: never imported by src/.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x approaches 2.
questions.explanation: Factorise: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = (x + 2)(x − 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2. As x → 2, this approaches 4.

mistakes.why: Substituting directly gives 0/0, which is undefined, not 0. Factorise first.

questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: limits and continuity (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: What is the derivative of sin x (x in radians)?
questions.explanation: d/dx (sin x) = cos x. The slope of the sine curve at any point equals the value of cosine there.

wrong.b: −cos x is the integral of sin x (plus c), not its derivative.
wrong.c: −sin x is the derivative of cos x.
wrong.d: tan x is sin x / cos x, not a derivative of sin x.

questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: differentiation (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Evaluate the integral of 3x² from x = 0 to x = 2.
questions.explanation: ∫ 3x² dx = x³. Evaluate from 0 to 2: 2³ − 0³ = 8.

mistakes.why: 12 is the derivative 6x at x = 2; integrate instead.
Divide by the new power: 3x³/3 = x³, not 3x³.

questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: integration (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Differentiate e^(2x) with respect to x.
questions.explanation: By the chain rule, d/dx e^(u) = e^(u) · du/dx. With u = 2x, du/dx = 2, so the derivative is 2e^(2x).

wrong.b: Multiply by the derivative of the inner function 2x, which is 2.
wrong.c: The power rule does not apply to exponentials; e^(u) differentiates to itself times u′.
wrong.d: Dividing by 2 is what integration does.

questions.objective: Apply the chain rule to exponential functions.
questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: differentiation (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Find the modulus of the complex number 3 + 4i.

mistakes.why: 7 adds the parts; the modulus is √(3² + 4²).
25 is |z|²; take the square root.

questions.objective: Find the modulus of a complex number.
questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: complex numbers (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level Further Maths).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows (2, 3) and (1, 4).
questions.explanation: For a 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d), the determinant is ad − bc = 2 × 4 − 3 × 1 = 5.

mistakes.why: 11 is ad + bc; subtract bc instead.
Order matters: ad − bc, not bc − ad.

questions.objective: Calculate the determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix.
questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: matrices (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Find the sum to infinity of the geometric series 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + …

wrong.b: 15 is the sum of only the first four terms.
wrong.d: A geometric series converges when |r| < 1, and here r = 1/2.

questions.objective: Find the sum to infinity of a convergent geometric series.
questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: sequences and series (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: True or false: f(x) = x³, for all real x, is a one-to-one function.
questions.explanation: x³ is strictly increasing, so different inputs always give different outputs. Any horizontal line meets its graph exactly once.

wrong.false: Unlike x², the function x³ never repeats a value: (−2)³ = −8 but 2³ = 8. It passes the horizontal line test.

questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: functions (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Evaluate ln(e³).
questions.explanation: ln is the inverse of eˣ, so ln(e³) = 3.

mistakes.why: 20.09 is e³ itself; the natural log undoes the exponential.

questions.objective: Use the inverse relationship between ln and e.
questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: exponential and logarithmic functions (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Select all the even functions, where f(−x) = f(x).
questions.explanation: (−x)² = x², cos(−x) = cos x and |−x| = |x|. Their graphs are symmetric about the y-axis.

wrong.d: sin(−x) = −sin x, so sin x is odd.

questions.objective: Classify functions as even or odd.
questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: functions (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Put the steps of a proof by mathematical induction in order.

options.text: Assume the statement is true for n = k
Conclude it is true for all positive integers n
Show the statement is true for n = 1
Show that it is then true for n = k + 1

questions.explanation: Base case (n = 1), inductive hypothesis (assume n = k), inductive step (prove n = k + 1), then the conclusion.
questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: proof (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level Further Maths).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.prompt: Find the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + x)⁵.
questions.explanation: The x² term is ⁵C₂ × x² = 10x², so the coefficient is 10.

mistakes.why: 5 is the coefficient of x (⁵C₁); for x² use ⁵C₂.
25 is 5²; use the binomial coefficient ⁵C₂ = 10.

questions.alignment: Pre-university mathematics: binomial expansion (e.g. STPM Mathematics (T) / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 4 m/s, in joules?
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 4² = 16 J.

mistakes.why: 8 is mv (momentum); kinetic energy uses ½mv².
Remember the ½: ½ × 2 × 16 = 16.

questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: work, energy and power (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: A 5 kg box is lifted 10 m. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², by how much does its gravitational potential energy increase, in joules?

mistakes.why: Multiply by g as well: mgh, not just mh.

questions.objective: Calculate changes in gravitational potential energy.
questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: work, energy and power (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: What fraction of a radioactive sample remains after 3 half-lives?
questions.explanation: Each half-life halves what is left: 1 → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8.

wrong.b: Decay halves the sample each time; it does not divide by the number of half-lives.

questions.objective: Use half-life to find the remaining fraction.
questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: radioactivity (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: A 6 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. What is the combined resistance in ohms?
questions.explanation: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω. A parallel combination is always less than the smallest resistor.

mistakes.why: 9 Ω is the series total; for parallel, add the reciprocals.
0.5 is 1/R; take the reciprocal to get R.

questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: direct current circuits (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: In the photoelectric effect, which change increases the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons?

options.text: Using light of a higher frequency
Using brighter light of the same frequency

questions.explanation: Each photon has energy hf. Higher frequency means more energy per photon, so KEmax = hf − φ increases.

wrong.b: Brighter light sends more photons, so more electrons are emitted, but each photon has the same energy.
wrong.c: Plate size changes how many electrons can be emitted, not their maximum energy.
wrong.d: Each electron absorbs one photon; waiting longer does not add energy to it.

questions.objective: Explain the photoelectric effect using photons.
questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: quantum physics (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: True or false: in simple harmonic motion, the acceleration is greatest at the equilibrium position.
questions.explanation: In SHM, a = −ω²x. Acceleration is proportional to displacement, so it is zero at equilibrium and greatest at the extremes (x = ±A). It is the speed that is greatest at equilibrium.

wrong.true: That describes speed, not acceleration. At equilibrium x = 0, so a = −ω²x = 0.

questions.objective: Describe how acceleration varies in SHM.
questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: oscillations (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: A 0.5 kg ball moves in a circle of radius 2 m at 4 m/s. What centripetal force acts on it, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Square the speed: v² = 16, not 4.
Divide by the radius: mv²/r.

questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: circular motion (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: Match each particle to its relative charge.
questions.explanation: Protons are positive (+1), electrons negative (−1) and neutrons neutral (0).
questions.objective: Recall the properties of subatomic particles.
questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: atomic structure (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: In a perfectly elastic collision between two objects, select all the quantities that are conserved.
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in every collision without external forces. In an elastic collision, total kinetic energy is conserved too.

wrong.c: Individual speeds usually change; only the totals are conserved.
wrong.d: Objects often bounce off in new directions.

questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: linear momentum (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: Light travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. Glass has a refractive index of 1.5. What is the speed of light in the glass, in units of 10⁸ m/s?

mistakes.why: 4.5 multiplies by n; light slows down in glass, so divide by n.

questions.objective: Relate refractive index to the speed of light.
questions.alignment: Pre-university physics: geometrical optics (e.g. STPM Physics / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: What is the shape of a methane (CH₄) molecule?
questions.explanation: Four bonding pairs around carbon repel each other equally, giving a tetrahedral shape with 109.5° bond angles.

wrong.b: Trigonal planar has three electron pairs, as in BF₃.
wrong.c: Linear has two electron pairs, as in CO₂.
wrong.d: Octahedral has six electron pairs, as in SF₆.

questions.objective: Predict molecular shapes using VSEPR theory.
questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: chemical bonding (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: What is the pH of 0.01 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (a strong acid)?
questions.explanation: HCl fully ionises, so [H⁺] = 0.01 = 10⁻² mol/dm³. pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] = 2.

mistakes.why: 0.01 is the hydrogen ion concentration; pH = −log₁₀ of it.
pH has a minus sign in front of the log: −log(10⁻²) = 2.

questions.objective: Calculate the pH of strong acids.
questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: ionic equilibria (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what happens to the equilibrium when the pressure is increased?

options.text: It shifts to the right, making more ammonia

questions.explanation: There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, so more NH₃ forms.

wrong.b: The left side has more gas moles; raising pressure favours fewer moles.
wrong.c: Pressure affects equilibria whenever the gas moles differ on each side.
wrong.d: An equilibrium is dynamic; changing pressure shifts it but does not stop it.

questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: chemical equilibrium (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: What is the oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄? (Enter the number, e.g. 7 for +7.)
questions.explanation: K is +1 and each O is −2. The compound is neutral: +1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0, so Mn = +7.

mistakes.why: Include potassium's +1: 1 + Mn − 8 = 0 gives Mn = +7.

questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: redox (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: Select all the alkanes.
questions.explanation: Alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: CH₄ (n = 1), C₃H₈ (n = 3) and C₄H₁₀ (n = 4).

wrong.b: C₂H₄ (ethene) fits CₙH₂ₙ: it is an alkene.
wrong.d: C₂H₂ (ethyne) fits CₙH₂ₙ₋₂: it is an alkyne.

questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: hydrocarbons (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the yield at equilibrium
It makes the reaction more exothermic
It is used up as the reaction goes

questions.explanation: A catalyst offers an alternative route with lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react.

wrong.b: A catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so the equilibrium position does not change.
wrong.c: The enthalpy change ΔH is the same with or without a catalyst.
wrong.d: A catalyst is regenerated at the end and not used up.

questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: reaction kinetics (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: Put these alkanes in order of boiling point, lowest first.
questions.explanation: Longer chains have more electrons and more surface contact, so stronger van der Waals forces and higher boiling points: methane < ethane < propane < butane.
questions.objective: Explain trends in boiling points of alkanes.
questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: hydrocarbons (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: True or false: all the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene are the same length.
questions.explanation: Benzene's π electrons are delocalised around the ring, so all six C–C bonds are identical, between a single and a double bond in length.

wrong.false: The alternating single/double (Kekulé) picture is not accurate; delocalisation makes all six bonds equal.

questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: arenes (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: An alkene reacts with hydrogen, using a nickel catalyst, to form an alkane. What is this reaction called?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen adds across the C=C double bond: this is hydrogenation, a type of addition reaction. It is used to make margarine from vegetable oils.
questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: alkenes (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: Match each functional group to its homologous series.
questions.explanation: C=C is the alkene group, −COOH the carboxylic acid group, and −COO− linking two chains is the ester group.
questions.alignment: Pre-university chemistry: organic chemistry (e.g. STPM Chemistry / A-level).

questions.subject: biology
questions.prompt: Where in a eukaryotic cell does the Krebs cycle take place?
questions.explanation: The Krebs cycle happens in the matrix of the mitochondrion.

wrong.c: The electron transport chain is on the inner membrane.
wrong.d: The stroma is where the Calvin cycle of photosynthesis happens.

questions.objective: Locate the stages of aerobic respiration.
questions.alignment: Pre-university biology: respiration (e.g. STPM Biology / A-level).

questions.subject: biology
questions.prompt: What is the net number of ATP molecules produced directly by glycolysis from one glucose molecule?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and makes 4 ATP, a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.

mistakes.why: 4 is the gross yield; 2 ATP are used at the start, so the net gain is 2.

questions.objective: Describe the energy yield of glycolysis.
questions.alignment: Pre-university biology: respiration (e.g. STPM Biology / A-level).

questions.subject: biology
questions.prompt: In DNA, which base pairs with adenine?
questions.explanation: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and guanine pairs with cytosine (three).

wrong.b: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, not DNA.

questions.alignment: Pre-university biology: nucleic acids (e.g. STPM Biology / A-level).

questions.subject: biology
questions.prompt: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of individuals show the recessive phenotype. What is the frequency of heterozygotes (as a decimal)?
questions.explanation: q² = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. Heterozygote frequency = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48.

mistakes.why: 0.24 is pq; heterozygotes are 2pq.
0.36 is p², the homozygous dominant frequency.

questions.alignment: Pre-university biology: population genetics (e.g. STPM Biology / A-level).

questions.subject: biology
questions.prompt: Put the stages of mitosis in order.
questions.explanation: Prophase (chromosomes condense), metaphase (line up at the equator), anaphase (chromatids pulled apart), telophase (new nuclei form). Remember PMAT.
questions.alignment: Pre-university biology: cell division (e.g. STPM Biology / A-level).

questions.subject: biology
questions.prompt: Select all the products of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Light energy splits water, releasing oxygen, and produces ATP and reduced NADP for the Calvin cycle.

wrong.d: Glucose is made later, from the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions).
wrong.e: Carbon dioxide is used in the Calvin cycle, not produced by the light-dependent reactions.

questions.alignment: Pre-university biology: photosynthesis (e.g. STPM Biology / A-level).

questions.subject: biology
questions.prompt: True or false: mRNA is made from DNA during translation.
questions.explanation: mRNA is made from DNA during transcription, in the nucleus. Translation happens at ribosomes, where mRNA is read to build a polypeptide.

wrong.true: Making mRNA from DNA is transcription; translation is using mRNA to make a protein.

questions.alignment: Pre-university biology: protein synthesis (e.g. STPM Biology / A-level).

questions.subject: biology
questions.prompt: Match each polymer to the monomer it is made from.
questions.explanation: Proteins are chains of amino acids, nucleic acids are chains of nucleotides, and starch is a chain of (α-)glucose.
questions.alignment: Pre-university biology: biological molecules (e.g. STPM Biology / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: According to the law of demand, when the price of a good rises (all else equal), what happens?

options.text: The demand curve shifts to the right

questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions: a movement up along the demand curve.

wrong.b: That would contradict the law of demand for normal goods.
wrong.c: A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; it does not shift it.
wrong.d: The law of demand is about buyers, not sellers.

questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: demand and supply (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: A good has a price elasticity of demand of −2. If its price rises by 10%, by what percentage does quantity demanded fall?
questions.explanation: PED = %Δ quantity ÷ %Δ price, so %Δ quantity = −2 × 10% = −20%. Quantity demanded falls by 20%.

mistakes.why: 5 is 10 ÷ 2; multiply the price change by the elasticity.

questions.objective: Use price elasticity of demand in calculations.
questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: elasticity (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: What is opportunity cost?

options.text: The value of the next best alternative given up
The money price paid for a good
The total cost of all alternatives
The cost of producing one more unit

questions.explanation: Choosing one thing means giving up the next best option. That forgone option is the opportunity cost.

wrong.b: The money price is only part of the picture; opportunity cost is about the alternative given up.
wrong.c: Only the next best alternative counts, not all of them.

questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: basic economic problem (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: Select all the factors of production.
questions.explanation: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital (man-made tools and machinery) and entrepreneurship.

wrong.d: Money is a medium of exchange, not a factor of production; in economics, "capital" means physical goods used to produce other goods.

questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: basic economic problem (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: True or false: a maximum price (price ceiling) set below the equilibrium price causes a shortage.
questions.explanation: At the lower price, consumers want to buy more and producers supply less, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage.

wrong.false: Below equilibrium, demand is higher and supply lower than at equilibrium, which is exactly a shortage. (A ceiling above equilibrium would have no effect.)

questions.objective: Analyse the effects of price controls.
questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: government intervention (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: Consumption = 500, investment = 200, government spending = 150, exports = 100 and imports = 120 (all in billions). Calculate GDP using the expenditure approach, in billions.

mistakes.why: Imports are subtracted, not added: use (X − M).
Imports were left out: subtract them too, 950 − 120 = 830.

questions.objective: Calculate GDP using the expenditure method.
questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: national income accounting (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: Which of these is a cause of demand-pull inflation?

options.text: A rapid rise in consumer spending
A rise in world oil prices

questions.explanation: Demand-pull inflation happens when aggregate demand grows faster than the economy's ability to produce, pulling prices up.

wrong.b: Higher oil prices raise production costs: that is cost-push inflation.
wrong.c: Higher interest rates reduce spending and usually lower inflation.
wrong.d: Falling wages lower costs and spending, which reduces inflation pressure.

questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: inflation (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: Match each description to its market structure.

left.text: A single seller with no close substitutes

questions.explanation: Perfect competition: many firms, identical goods. Monopoly: one seller. Oligopoly: a few big firms that react to each other's decisions.
questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: market structures (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: A central bank raises interest rates. What is the usual aim?
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates make borrowing dearer and saving more attractive, reducing spending and easing inflation.

wrong.b: Government spending is fiscal policy, decided by the government, not the central bank.
wrong.d: Higher rates usually strengthen the currency by attracting foreign savings.

questions.objective: Explain the effects of monetary policy.
questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: monetary policy (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).

questions.subject: economics
questions.prompt: What is the name for the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year?
questions.explanation: Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the value of everything produced within a country's borders in a period.
questions.alignment: Pre-university economics: national income (e.g. STPM Economics / A-level).
